unit_label: BRBL::MOD_D::U17: Distinguish private,public and one-person companies

payload.title: Private does not mean unincorporated
payload.core_explanation_md:
Private-company articles restrict share transfer, limit membership under the stated two-hundred-member rule with its statutory counting qualifications, and prohibit public invitations for securities. The ordinary formation minimum is two members; the one-person company is the recognised single-member form. A public company has the stated seven-person formation minimum. A public company is not necessarily listed on an exchange.

An OPC includes the prescribed nominee arrangement for death or incapacity of its member. Do not reuse the textbook compulsory-conversion capital/turnover figures or its obsolete private/public commencement comparison as current law. Verify current rules for eligibility, conversion and commencement separately. The legal form, listing status and particular compliance obligation are distinct questions.

self_check.prompt_text: Is every public company necessarily exchange-listed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Public-company status and listing differ.

payload.stem_md: A company is public but its securities are not exchange-listed. Is that classification inherently inconsistent?

options.text_md: Yes, every public company must already be listed
No, public status alone does not establish listing
Yes, it must be an ordinary partnership
No, because every private company may invite public subscriptions

payload.stem_md: A single-member incorporated company has the prescribed nominee arrangement. Which form is being described?

options.text_md: A public company formed by seven members
A statutory corporation created only by special legislation

options.explanation_md: The single-member form and nominee arrangement fit the described framework.
